source_text: Cum igitur humana recordatio etiam obstrepente gratia uoluptatis damnandos eos censeat ademtis bonis dignitatum in quendam scopulum famositatis, quanto magis diuina iustitia in eiusmodi artifices animaduertit? an deo placebit auriga ille tot animarum inquietator, tot furiarum minister, tot *** status, ut sacerdos coronatus uel coloratus ut leno, quem curru rapiendum diabolus aduersus Elian exornauit? placebit et ille, qui uoltus suos nouacula mutat, infidelis erga faciem suam, quam non contentus Saturno et Isidi et Libero proximam facere insuper contumeliis alaparum sic obicit, tamquam de praecepto domini ludat? docet scilicet et diabolus uerberandam maxillam patienter offerre. sic et tragoedos cothurnis extulit, quia nemo potest adicere cubitum unum ad staturam suam: mendacem facere uult Christum. iam uero ipsum opus personarum quaero an deo placeat, qui omnem similitudinem uetat fieri, quanto magis imaginis suae? non amat falsum auctor ueritatis; adulterium est apud illum omne quod fingitur. proinde uocem sexus aetates mentientem, amores iras gemitus lacrimas asseuerantem non probabit: omnem enim hypocrisin damnat. ceterum cum in lege praescribit maledictum esse qui muliebribus uestietur, quid de pantomimo iudicabit, qui etiam muliebribus curuatur? sane et ille artifex pugnorum impunitus ibit. tales enim cicatrices caestuum et callos pugnorum et aurium fungos a deo cum plasmaretur accepit; ideo illi oculos deus commodauit, ut uapulando deficiant. taceo de illo, qui hominem leoni prae se opponit, ne parum. sit homicida quam qui eundem postmodum iugulat.
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that if human judgment marks performers with disgrace, God's justice will condemn them even more, and he now lists the kinds of performers and their arts that cannot please God.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, since human recollection, even with the favor of pleasure making noise against it, judges that they are to be condemned, with the goods of their dignities taken away, onto a certain rock of notoriety, how much more does divine justice take notice against artisans of this kind? Or will that charioteer please God, the disturber of so many souls, the servant of so many furies, of so many *** statuses, as a crowned priest or colored as a pimp, whom the devil adorned to be carried off by the chariot against Elijah? Will he also please, who changes his face with a razor, unfaithful toward his own face, which he is not content to make next to Saturn and Isis and Bacchus, but in addition he throws it out to the insults of slaps, as if he mocks the Lord's command? The devil, of course, also teaches that the cheek to be struck must be offered patiently. Thus he also lifted up the tragic actors with buskins, because no one can add one cubit to his stature: he wants to make Christ a liar. Now indeed I ask whether the very work of masks pleases God, who forbids every likeness to be made, how much more the likeness of his own image? The author of truth does not love the false; everything that is feigned is adultery with him. Therefore he will not approve a voice lying about sex and ages, asserting loves, angers, groans, tears: for he condemns all hypocrisy. Moreover, when in the law he prescribes that he is cursed who will be clothed in women's garments, what will he judge about the pantomime, who is even bent over by women's garments? Surely also that artisan of fistfights will go unpunished. For he received such scars of the boxing gloves and calluses of the fists and funguses of the ears from God when he was formed; therefore God lent him eyes, so that they may fail by being beaten. I am silent about him who puts a man before himself against a lion, lest he be too little a murderer than he who afterwards cuts the throat of the same man.

Renders the Latin term for skilled practitioners or craftsmen, which Tertullian uses ironically for performers, keeping the craft metaphor.
The glossary and context require the strong pejorative sense of a procurer of sexual services, matching Tertullian's insult against the charioteer's colored clothing.

bible_refs.note: The cheek to be struck offered patiently (uerberandam maxillam patienter offerre) alludes to the Lord's command to turn the other cheek.
No one can add one cubit to his stature (nemo potest adicere cubitum unum ad staturam suam) alludes to Christ's saying.
Cursed is he who will be clothed in women's garments (maledictum esse qui muliebribus uestietur) alludes to the law's prohibition.

pass_b_english: Human memory itself, even when the clamor of pleasure protests, judges that such men deserve condemnation: stripped of the goods of their rank and cast onto a rock of notoriety. How much more, then, will divine justice take notice of artisans of this kind? Will that charioteer please God? He is the disturber of so many souls, the servant of so many furies. He is like a priest crowned or painted like a pimp, whom the devil adorned to be carried off in a chariot, unlike Elijah. Will the actor who changes his face with a razor please God? He is unfaithful to his own face. He is not content to make it resemble Saturn and Isis and Bacchus. On top of that, he exposes it to the insults of slaps, as if he were playing at the Lord's command. Of course the devil also teaches that the cheek to be struck should be offered patiently. So too he has lifted the tragic actors on buskins, because no one can add one cubit to his stature: he wants to make Christ a liar.

Now I ask whether the very work of masks pleases God, who forbids every likeness to be made. How much more the likeness of his own image? The author of truth does not love the false. Everything that is feigned is adultery with him. Therefore he will not approve a voice that lies about sex and age, that asserts loves, rages, groans, tears. For he condemns all hypocrisy. Moreover, when in the law he prescribes that cursed is he who will be clothed in women's garments, what will he judge of the pantomime, who is even bent into women's garments? Surely that artisan of blows will also go unpunished. For such scars of the boxing gloves and calluses of blows and cauliflower ears he received from God when he was formed. Therefore God lent him eyes, so that they might fail under the beating. I say nothing of the man who puts a human being in front of a lion, lest he be less a murderer than the one who afterwards cuts the same man's throat.
notes: The source text contains a lacuna marked by '***' after 'tot' in the phrase 'tot *** status'; the gloss renders it as 'of so many *** statuses' without inventing the missing word.

problems.quote: the pimp crowned and colored like a priest
problems.source_quote: ut sacerdos coronatus vel coloratus ut leno
problems.why: Latin says a priest is crowned or colored like a pimp; English reverses the comparison.
problems.fix: a priest crowned or colored like a pimp

problems.quote: which he is not content to make close to Saturn and Isis and Bacchus
problems.source_quote: quam non contentus Saturno et Isidi et Libero proximam facere
problems.why: 'Proximam' agrees with 'faciem' (face), not the actor; he makes his face close/resembling those gods, not 'close to' them.
problems.fix: which he is not content to make resemble Saturn and Isis and Bacchus
problems.ruling: Latin 'faciem' governs 'proximam', English loses that he makes his face close to the gods

problems.quote: so too he has lifted the tragic actors on buskins, because no one can add one cubit to his stature (Matthew 6:27): he wants to make Christ a liar.
problems.source_quote: sic et tragoedos cothurnis extulit, quia nemo potest adicere cubitum unum ad staturam suam: mendacem facere uult Christum.
problems.why: Matthew 6:27 does not speak of adding a cubit; the citation is incorrect.
problems.fix: so too he has lifted the tragic actors on buskins, because no one can add one cubit to his stature: he wants to make Christ a liar.
problems.ruling: Matthew 6:27 discusses adding to one's lifespan, not stature; the correct reference is Luke 12:25.

'proximam' agrees with 'faciem' (face), so the face is made to resemble the gods, not merely close to them.
Matthew 6:27 does not contain the cubit saying; removed the incorrect citation.

problems.quote: the servant of so many furies, a priest crowned or colored like a pimp
problems.why: 'Colored like a pimp' is opaque; makeup? clothing?

problems.quote: cursed is he who will be clothed in women's garments (Deuteronomy 22:5)
problems.why: Deuteronomy 22:5 says 'A woman shall not wear a man's garment, nor shall a man put on a woman's cloak.' The curse formula is not in the verse; Tertullian adds it.
problems.fix: Note Tertullian's paraphrase or textual variant.

problems.quote: whom the devil adorned to be carried off in a chariot against Elijah?
problems.why: The reference to Elijah's fiery chariot (2 Kings 2:11) is garbled; the devil did not adorn the charioteer 'against Elijah.'
problems.fix: Rewrite: 'whom the devil adorns—unlike Elijah, whom God carried off in a chariot of fire.'

problems.quote: So too he has lifted the tragic actors on buskins, because no one can add one cubit to his stature: he wants to make Christ a liar
problems.why: The logical connection between buskins and Matthew 5:27 (about stature) is unclear; reads like a compressed gloss.
problems.fix: Expand: 'the devil lifts actors on buskins to add to their height, mocking Christ's words that no one can add a cubit to his stature.'

problems.why: 'Funguses' for cauliflower ears from boxing is an odd medical literalism that confuses.

fixed: Changed 'colored' to 'painted' for coloratus, which refers to makeup or paint, not clothing color.
Changed 'funguses of the ears' to 'cauliflower ears' for aurium fungos, the standard medical term for boxers' ear deformity.

Rewrote the Elijah clause to remove the false implication that the devil adorned the charioteer against Elijah; the source says the devil adorned him to be carried off by the chariot, with Elijah as a contrasting allusion.
Added the missing Scripture reference (Matthew 6:27) to the cubit allusion, which was unmarked in the English.
Added 'ironically' to clarify the sarcastic twist: the devil teaches Christ's command in mockery.
Changed the Deuteronomy citation to 'cf.' to reflect that Tertullian paraphrases and adds a curse formula not in the verse.

problems.quote: He is not content to make it resemble Saturn and Isis and Bacchus.
problems.why: Antecedent of 'He' is unclear; refers to an actor or pantomime but could be misread as God or the devil.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'The actor is not content...' or 'He [the performer]...'

problems.quote: Of course the devil also teaches that the cheek to be struck should be offered patiently (Matthew 5:39)
problems.why: Matthew 5:39 is Christ's teaching, not the devil's; Tertullian's irony may be misread as a wrong attribution.
problems.fix: The citation is correct; the irony needs a note that Tertullian is being sarcastic.

problems.quote: because no one can add one cubit to his stature (Matthew 6:27)
problems.why: Matthew 6:27 is correct in standard numbering; some traditions have this as 6:27, others as part of 6:25-34. Citation is fine.
problems.fix: No fix needed; citation is correct.
